theory.intro: To find a probability for a sample mean, standardise with $z=\dfrac{\bar{x}-\mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}$. The divisor is the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$, not of one observation, so a sample mean sits much closer to $\mu$ than a single value does.
facts: By the central limit theorem $\bar{X}$ is approximately $N\left(\mu,\dfrac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$ when the sample is random and $n\ge 30$.
Standardise a **single observation** with $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, using $\sigma$ and no $\sqrt{n}$.
Read the stem carefully: one observation and a sample mean give different $z$ values from the same number.
$P(\bar{X}>\mu)=0.5$, because the sampling distribution is symmetrical about $\mu$.
Because $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ is small, a sample mean only a little away from $\mu$ can be very unlikely.
Shade the required region on the curve of $\bar{X}$ first, because the probability is the area of the shaded part.
steps: Write the mean and the standard deviation $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$ of $\bar{X}$
Shade the region on the curve and find its area

foundation.question_text:
A population has mean $500$ g and standard deviation $60$ g. A random sample of $36$ items is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** exceeds $520$ g, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $64$ and standard deviation $35$.

A population has mean $120$ and standard deviation $18$.
A random sample of $81$ values gives a sample mean of $123$.
Find the $z$-score of this sample mean.

A population has mean $60$ and standard deviation $12$.
Find the $z$-score of the value $66$ when it is a single observation, and the $z$-score of $66$ when it is the mean of a random sample of $36$ values.
foundation.solution_text:
For a single observation the divisor is $\sigma$.
$z=\dfrac{66-60}{12}$
$=0.5$
For a sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{36}}=2$.
$z=\dfrac{66-60}{2}$
$=3$

development.question_text:
A population has mean $95$ and standard deviation $20$.
A random sample of $100$ values is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** exceeds $98$, using this table.
$\begin{array}{c|c} z & P(Z<z) \\ \hline 0.60 & 0.7257 \\ 1.10 & 0.8643 \\ 1.50 & 0.9332 \\ 2.40 & 0.9918 \end{array}$

A population has mean $155$ and standard deviation $45$.
A random sample of $225$ values is taken.

$\begin{array}{c|c} z & P(Z<z) \\ \hline 0.50 & 0.6915 \\ 0.80 & 0.7881 \\ 1.20 & 0.8849 \\ 2.10 & 0.9821 \end{array}$

A population has mean $500$ and standard deviation $40$.
A random sample of $100$ values is taken.
Find the probability that the **sample mean** lies between $496$ and $504$, using the empirical rule.

A population has mean $25$ and standard deviation $6$.
A random sample of $144$ values gives a sample mean of $26.2$.
Find the $z$-score of this sample mean.

A population has mean $800$ and standard deviation $50$.
State which is smaller, the probability that a single observation exceeds $810$ or the probability that the mean of a random sample of $100$ observations exceeds $810$.
Support your answer with the two $z$-scores.
development.solution_text:
For a single observation the divisor is $\sigma=50$.
$z=\dfrac{810-800}{50}$
$=0.2$
For the sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{50}{\sqrt{100}}=5$.
$z=\dfrac{810-800}{5}$
$=2$
A larger $z$ leaves a smaller right tail, so the probability for the sample mean is smaller.

mastery.question_text:
A population has mean $70$ and standard deviation $16$.
Find the sample size $n$ for which the standard deviation of $\bar{X}$ is $2$, and then use the empirical rule to find $P(\bar{X}>74)$ for that sample size.

A population has mean $250$ and standard deviation $36$.
Random samples of size $81$ are taken.
Find the interval, symmetrical about the mean, inside which $95\%$ of the sample means lie.
mastery.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\dfrac{36}{\sqrt{81}}$
$=4$
The central $95\%$ runs from $z=-2$ to $z=2$.
$250-2\times 4=242$
$250+2\times 4=258$
$95\%$ of sample means lie between $242$ and $258$.

mastery.question_text:
The volume of juice poured by a machine has mean $6.4$ mL per second and standard deviation $1.2$ mL per second.
Find the probability that a single reading exceeds $6.8$, and the probability that the mean of a random sample of $36$ readings exceeds $6.8$.
Round each $z$-score to two decimal places and use this table.
$\begin{array}{c|c} z & P(Z<z) \\ \hline 0.33 & 0.6293 \\ 0.67 & 0.7486 \\ 1.00 & 0.8413 \\ 2.00 & 0.9772 \end{array}$
mastery.solution_text:
For a single reading the divisor is $\sigma=1.2$.
$z=\dfrac{6.8-6.4}{1.2}$
$=0.33$
$P(X>6.8)=1-0.6293$
$=0.3707$
For the sample mean the divisor is $\dfrac{1.2}{\sqrt{36}}=0.2$.
$z=\dfrac{6.8-6.4}{0.2}$
$=2$
$P(\bar{X}>6.8)=1-0.9772$
$=0.0228$
